transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because I just can’t seem to keep my mind on things the way I used to. I mean, I'll be sitting at my desk, staring at a loan worksheet or a client follow-up list, and I just reread the same line over and over. And then I end up putting off making calls because even simple decisions feel so much harder than they should. It's frustrating because I’ve been a loan officer for years, and I usually know these forms like the back of my hand. Speaking of hands, my knuckles have been aching lately. I don't know if it's arthritis or just the weather changing. My sister gets terrible arthritis when it rains, and she lives up in Seattle, so you can imagine how often she complains about it. Anyway, where was I? Oh, right, work. Yeah, it's just... everything feels like it takes twice as much effort to figure out.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, most days, even when things are going okay at work or home?

Well, yes, I suppose so. Most days there’s just this... this dull heaviness sitting with me. It doesn't really seem to matter if it's a good day or a bad day. Like, even when I’m out in my garden. I used to spend hours out there. I have these big hydrangeas along the back fence, though this year I think the soil pH is all wrong because they’re coming in pink instead of that deep blue I like. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she swears by mixing used coffee grounds into the dirt for that. She drinks this terribly bitter dark roast—gets it shipped in special from some little shop all the way in New Orleans, can you believe that? The shipping alone must cost a fortune, and she's on a fixed income, but she won't drink anything else. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Even when I'm out there trying to tend to the flowers, or when I'm over at the community center... those are places that really used to lift me up, you know? Now I just feel like I’m going through the motions. I just have this smile pasted on for everyone, but underneath, that heaviness is just always there.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about different things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to worry, and does it feel hard to control those thoughts?

Worrying? No, not really. I mean, I don't sit around chewing my nails over things for no reason. I worry about normal things, I suppose. Like if the grocery store is going to be out of my favorite paper towels again. They’ve been having all sorts of stocking issues lately, and I really only like the ones with the select-a-size sheets. My daughter, she just buys the cheapest brand she can find, and they completely fall apart the second they touch a wet spill. She has these beautiful granite countertops she put in last spring—paid an absolute fortune for them, too. But the contractor she hired, oh, he was a real piece of work. He left his big ugly truck parked in her driveway for three days straight while he went fishing down in the Keys. Can you imagine the nerve? Just left it there, leaking oil all over her new driveway pavers. She actually had to threaten to call a tow company to get him to move it. 

But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, worrying. No, my mind doesn't really race or spin out of control with worries. It's really just that heavy, tired feeling I told you about.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or that it's harder to get yourself going, like your body is dragging even when you're not physically tired?

Moving slower? No, I don't think so. I mean, I feel heavy, like I said, but my body isn't dragging around in slow motion or anything. 

Now, if you want to talk about moving slowly, you should see the new girl they hired at the branch, Brittany. I swear, it takes her ten minutes just to staple a closing packet together. She spends half the morning on her phone watching those little videos of people making recipes. She showed me one yesterday where they made a whole lasagna in a slow cooker. A slow cooker! Can you imagine? The noodles must get absolutely mushy. My mother used to make the best lasagna, with the ricotta and a homemade sauce she'd simmer on the stove all Sunday afternoon. She grew her own tomatoes for it, too. Big, beautiful beefsteak tomatoes right in the backyard... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, dragging. No, I don't think my body is moving any slower than I usually do.
How long have you been feeling this way — the heaviness, loss of interest, and difficulty focusing — and has it been going on every day, most days, or only occasionally?

How long? Well, let me think... it's been a while now. I'd say it started a little over two years ago, right after my close friend passed away. We used to do everything together, you know? She was the one who actually convinced me to get my associate's degree when we were in our thirties. We took night classes at the community college. Oh, the parking there was just atrocious. You had to get there a full hour early just to find a spot that wasn't halfway to the next county. And the lighting in those parking lots! I used to carry this little pepper spray on my keychain because it was so dark walking back to the car. Not that I ever had to use it, thank goodness. I think I ended up throwing it away last year because it expired. Does pepper spray even expire? I suppose the aerosol part of it might lose its pressure. My brother-in-law, he's one of those doomsday prepper types, he has a whole basement full of canned beans and water jugs. He rotate them out every six months, which seems like a full-time job in itself. He even bought this massive generator that runs on... what is it, propane? Or diesel? I can't remember. 

Anyway, um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, how long I've felt this way. Yes, it's been pretty much most days for the last two years, ever since she died. Just that same heaviness.
Would you say that most days, your mood is significantly lower than it used to be, even when there’s no obvious reason for it?

Lower mood? Yes, I suppose so. Most days there’s just this... this dull heaviness sitting with me, even if absolutely nothing has gone wrong. Like when I go down to the community center. I used to love it there, but lately... well, to be fair, they did just repaint the main hall this absolutely dreadful shade of yellow. I think the flyer called it "harvest gold," but it looks exactly like the kitchen appliances everyone had back in the seventies. My Aunt Martha had a refrigerator that exact color, and it hummed so loudly you couldn't even hear yourself think while you were trying to eat your breakfast. She lived in this tiny little duplex over in Springfield, and the neighbors there were always causing a racket, playing that thumping music at all hours of the night. I don't know how she slept through it. She was practically deaf in her right ear, though, from working at the textile mill when she was young. They didn't have all those OSHA safety regulations back then, you know. People just lost their hearing and that was that. 

Anyway... gosh, what was the question? I'm sorry, my mind just wandered right off. Oh, right, my mood being lower. Yes, it's just that constant heaviness. Even when I’m at the community center, or out in my garden pulling weeds—places that really used to lift me up and make me feel good—I just feel like I’m going through the motions now. I'm just standing there with a smile pasted on my face, but I don't really feel it.
Do you find that you have significantly less energy than before, or that even small tasks feel exhausting, most days?

Less energy? Oh, definitely. I wake up tired even after a full night of sleep. By the time I’ve done just a couple of client calls for work... like yesterday, I was going over a debt consolidation plan with this couple, and they had four different department store credit cards maxed out. I just don't understand why people sign up for those. The interest rates are absolute highway robbery! Usually twenty-nine percent or more. My niece, Sarah, got roped into one at that big makeup store at the mall. They offered her a free canvas tote bag, and the next thing you know, she's paying thirty dollars a month in interest just on lipsticks and lotions. I told her, I said, "Sarah, a cheap bag is not worth ruining your credit score before you even turn twenty-five." She didn't listen, of course. Young people just tap their phones to pay now and don't even look at the numbers. I still balance my checkbook every Sunday evening at the kitchen table. I have a special green pen I use just for the deposits... 

Oh, dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Right, feeling exhausted. Yes. Like I was saying, even after just those few client calls, or just going out back to water the tomatoes, my body feels like I’ve put in a whole day already. I'm just completely drained by the smallest things.
Do you often feel like you're not good enough, or find yourself dwelling on past mistakes, even when there's no clear reason to feel that way?

Not good enough? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really sit around beating myself up or feeling worthless, if that's what you mean. I know I'm good at my job, even if I don't have the energy for it right now. I've been doing it for almost thirty years. Started out as a bank teller, actually, back when they still had the pneumatic tubes at the drive-through. Remember those? You'd put your check in the little plastic canister and it would go *whoosh* right up into the ceiling. My son used to love watching that when he was little. He'd always ask for a lollipop, and the teller would send one back down the tube. They don't do that anymore. Now it's all ATMs and mobile deposits. Half the time you can't even get a real person on the phone if you have a problem with your account. You just get this automated voice telling you to press one for this and two for that, and then it hangs up on you anyway. It's so frustrating. I spent forty-five minutes on hold with the cable company last week just trying to get them to explain a five-dollar charge on my bill. Five dollars! And the music they play while you're waiting... it's like this electronic elevator music that just repeats the same four notes over and over...

Wait, I'm sorry. I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling like I'm not good enough or dwelling on mistakes. No, I don't really have that problem. I just feel heavy and tired all the time.
Do you ever feel restless, keyed up, or on edge, to the point where you have trouble sitting still or calming your mind, even if just for a few minutes?

Restless or on edge? No, not really. I don't feel keyed up like that. I'm usually just too tired to be restless, to be honest. But speaking of trouble sitting still, my neighbor's dog—it's this little terrier mix, scruffy little thing—it absolutely cannot sit still. They leave it out in the yard all day while they're at work, and it just paces the fence line, back and forth, back and forth, yapping at every single car that goes by. And let me tell you, we live on a corner lot, so there are a lot of cars. The mail carrier won't even come up to their porch anymore. He just leaves their packages at the edge of the driveway because the dog nipped at his pant leg last month. I saw the whole thing from my kitchen window. I was washing out my coffee pot—I always use one of those French presses, you know, the glass ones? The coffee just tastes so much richer than those plastic drip machines. Although, they are a pain to clean. You have to scoop all the wet grounds out by hand, and if you wash them down the sink, they clog up the garbage disposal. My plumber, Gary, told me that coffee grounds and eggshells are the worst things you can put down a drain. He charged me two hundred dollars last time he had to come snake my pipes...

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry. What was it you were asking me about? Restless? Right, no. I don't feel restless or on edge. Just... just that heavy, tired feeling I mentioned before. None of that keyed-up business.
Have you ever found yourself feeling guilty about things that you normally wouldn't, or like you're letting people down even when there's no real reason to feel that way?

Guilty? Like I'm letting people down? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really have those kinds of feelings. I mean, I do my job, I pay my bills... speaking of bills, did you know the post office is raising the price of stamps again? It's just ridiculous. I remember when a stamp was, what, thirty-two cents? Now it's practically a dollar just to mail a birthday card. And the cards themselves! I went to the pharmacy the other day to get a card for my sister's anniversary, and they wanted seven dollars and fifty cents for a piece of cardboard with some glitter on it. Seven fifty! I could buy a whole rotisserie chicken at the grocery store for that. And the chickens at the new market down the street are really quite good. They season them with this lemon pepper rub. My husband used to love lemon pepper on everything. We used to have it on baked tilapia every Friday night, with a side of steamed asparagus. You have to be careful not to over-steam the asparagus, though, or it gets all mushy and stringy... 

Oh, my. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I'm so sorry, my mind just wanders. You were asking about feeling guilty? Right. No, I don't really feel guilty or anything like that. Just the tiredness, really.

Not good enough? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really sit around beating myself up or feeling worthless, if that's what you mean. I know I'm good at my job, even if I don't have the energy for it right now. I've been doing it for almost thirty years. Started out as a bank teller, actually, back when they still had the pneumatic tubes at the drive-through. Remember those? You'd put your check in the little plastic canister and it would go *whoosh* right up into the ceiling. My son used to love watching that when he was little. He'd always ask for a lollipop, and the teller would send one back down the tube. They don't do that anymore. Now it's all ATMs and mobile deposits. Half the time you can't even get a real person on the phone if you have a problem with your account. You just get this automated voice telling you to press one for this and two for that, and then it hangs up on you anyway. It's so frustrating. I spent forty-five minutes on hold with the cable company last week just trying to get them to explain a five-dollar charge on my bill. Five dollars! And the music they play while you're waiting... it's like this electronic elevator music that just repeats the same four notes over and over...

Wait, I'm sorry. I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling like I'm not good enough or dwelling on mistakes. No, I don't really have that problem. I just feel heavy and tired all the time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences psychomotor agitation or restlessness, which would point more strongly toward a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F33.1) if present, and help differentiate from persistent depressive disorder (F43.22).
doctor.question: Do you ever feel restless, keyed up, or on edge, to the point where you have trouble sitting still or calming your mind, even if just for a few minutes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of restlessness, feeling keyed up, or being on edge (symptoms of anxiety or psychomotor agitation). My symptom profile does not include any symptoms matching this description (it includes Depressed Mood, Fatigue, Diminished Thinking, Hopelessness, Functional Impairment, and Duration).

patient.answer:
Restless or on edge? No, not really. I don't feel keyed up like that. I'm usually just too tired to be restless, to be honest. But speaking of trouble sitting still, my neighbor's dog—it's this little terrier mix, scruffy little thing—it absolutely cannot sit still. They leave it out in the yard all day while they're at work, and it just paces the fence line, back and forth, back and forth, yapping at every single car that goes by. And let me tell you, we live on a corner lot, so there are a lot of cars. The mail carrier won't even come up to their porch anymore. He just leaves their packages at the edge of the driveway because the dog nipped at his pant leg last month. I saw the whole thing from my kitchen window. I was washing out my coffee pot—I always use one of those French presses, you know, the glass ones? The coffee just tastes so much richer than those plastic drip machines. Although, they are a pain to clean. You have to scoop all the wet grounds out by hand, and if you wash them down the sink, they clog up the garbage disposal. My plumber, Gary, told me that coffee grounds and eggshells are the worst things you can put down a drain. He charged me two hundred dollars last time he had to come snake my pipes...

Oh, goodness, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry. What was it you were asking me about? Restless? Right, no. I don't feel restless or on edge. Just... just that heavy, tired feeling I mentioned before. None of that keyed-up business.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences feelings of worthlessness or inappropriate guilt, which would support a diagnosis of major depressive disorder (F33.1) over adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself feeling guilty about things that you normally wouldn't, or like you're letting people down even when there's no real reason to feel that way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of excessive or inappropriate guilt, which is not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Like I'm letting people down? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really have those kinds of feelings. I mean, I do my job, I pay my bills... speaking of bills, did you know the post office is raising the price of stamps again? It's just ridiculous. I remember when a stamp was, what, thirty-two cents? Now it's practically a dollar just to mail a birthday card. And the cards themselves! I went to the pharmacy the other day to get a card for my sister's anniversary, and they wanted seven dollars and fifty cents for a piece of cardboard with some glitter on it. Seven fifty! I could buy a whole rotisserie chicken at the grocery store for that. And the chickens at the new market down the street are really quite good. They season them with this lemon pepper rub. My husband used to love lemon pepper on everything. We used to have it on baked tilapia every Friday night, with a side of steamed asparagus. You have to be careful not to over-steam the asparagus, though, or it gets all mushy and stringy... 

Oh, my. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I'm so sorry, my mind just wanders. You were asking about feeling guilty? Right. No, I don't really feel guilty or anything like that. Just the tiredness, really.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms have persisted for over two years, with a depressed mood, loss of interest, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. There is no significant evidence of anxiety, restlessness, guilt, or slowed psychomotor function. The chronic nature and constellation of symptoms align more strongly with F33.1 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder, current episode severe without psychotic symptoms) than with F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood), which has been ruled out due to the duration and severity of symptoms.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating, all of which have been present for over two years since the death of a close friend. These symptoms align with the diagnostic criteria for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). Other candidates, such as major depressive disorder (F33.1 was already selected as the best fit), generalized anxiety disorder (F48.1), and persistent complex bereavement (F34.1), were considered but ruled out due to lack of excessive worry, absence of trauma-related symptoms, and the chronic, non-episodic nature of the condition.
